Summary: - Retain existing bat roosts and access points within developments; studies reported similar numbers of bats continuing to roost post-renovation, maternity use at some retained roosts, and higher likelihood of use than newly created roosts (ID: 947). - Relocate roost access points where necessary; evidence shows mixed use, with low use of a ‘bend’ design but increased roost use after installing a ‘straight’ access design (ID: 946). - Create alternative roosts within developments (e.g., bat boxes, lofts, barns, purpose-built roosts); uptake varied: some alternatives were not used, others were used at 13–74% of sites, maternity use occurred at one of 19 sites, and post-destruction colonies sometimes used purpose-built roosts in higher or similar numbers though often in lower numbers; retained roosts were more likely to be used than new ones (ID: 949). - Legally protect bats during development via licensing; reviews showed increased licensing, limited post-development monitoring, frequent destruction of roosts under licence, and variable uptake of compensation roosts (31–67% used; five of 28 used with two by similar or greater numbers) (ID: 1935). - Conserve roosting sites in old structures or buildings by adapting them (e.g., install access grilles, attach wood, clear debris, or box-in roosts); studies recorded increased hibernating numbers in some cases, multi-species use after clearance, and continued but reduced use when a roost was boxed-in (ID: 2046). - Provide training to conservationists, land managers, and the development sector on bat ecology and conservation; no studies have evaluated the effects of this action (ID: 997).

Summary: Evidence from five studies across the USA, Germany, South Africa, Israel and Mexico reported that creating artificial water sources resulted in bat activity (relative abundance) being similar or higher over reservoirs and waste water treatment pools, heliponds and drainage ditches, retention ponds and farm/cattle ponds compared to natural wetlands, nearby vineyards, surrounding forest or grassland/crops, trees and orchards; one study found a similar number of bat species over farm ponds and in other nearby habitats [959]. Two studies in the USA found that managing livestock water troughs as drinking resources increased bat use: removing livestock modifications increased drinking frequency and reduced the number of approaches before successful drinking, and larger, full tanks with sparse surrounding vegetation had more bats drinking than smaller, half-full tanks with no or dense surrounding vegetation [1951]. No studies were found that evaluated the effects on bats of changing effluent treatments used in agriculture and forestry [1016], or of managing ditches to benefit bats [1944].

Summary: Bat gantries: Across three studies (UK and France), two replicated UK studies found fewer bats used gantries than crossed the road below at traffic height and one gantry was not used at all; a replicated study in France recorded use by three bat species/species groups, but almost half of crossing bats still flew over the road at other locations [978]. Overpasses: Four studies reported mixed outcomes—an Australian site comparison found the same number of bat species at an overpass as in nearby forest and bushland [977]; two replicated studies in Ireland and France recorded use by two or three species/species groups, but up to three-quarters of bats crossed the road below at traffic height or at other nearby locations [977]; one UK study found an overpass with planters was used by two-thirds of crossing bats, whereas an unvegetated overpass with a paved road over it was not used by crossing bats [977]. Green bridges: One UK study found a green bridge was used by 97% of bats crossing a road [979].
